bib.title: ChatGPT's One-year Anniversary: Are Open-Source Large Language Models Catching up?
bib.venue: preprint (page 1 footer: 'Preprint. Under review.'; arXiv:2311.16989v4 [cs.CL] 15 Jan 2024)

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed only for lineage.

question: On which tasks has an open-source LLM claimed parity with or superiority over ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo) one year after its release?
hypothesis: Open-source LLMs are quickly catching up with ChatGPT and already match or beat it on some benchmarks (implied by abstract and introduction).
contributions: Consolidating various evaluations of open-source LLMs, providing an unbiased and comprehensive view of open-source LLMs vs. ChatGPT (Figure 1, Section 3.1).
Systematically reviewing open-source LLMs that match or surpass the performance of ChatGPT in various tasks with analysis (Figure 2, Section 3, Section 4.2); live web page maintained.
Presenting insights on the trend of open-source LLMs development (Section 4.1), the good practices to train open-source LLMs (Section 4.3) and potential issues with open-source LLMs (Section 4.4).

limits: No experiments of its own: every number is copied from the original model papers or leaderboards, so judge model, prompt, shot count, decoding and benchmark version differ per cell and are not stated.

Selection is by claim: it surveys tasks where an open model 'has claimed' parity or better, so it is biased towards positive cases; the abstract says as much ('surveying all tasks where an open-source LLM has claimed to be on par or better').

The comparator is GPT-3.5-turbo, a moving target: the intro notes closed models are retrained and ChatGPT behaviour changes over time (Chen et al. 2023d), so a score on one date is not comparable to one on another. No snapshot or date is given for the GPT-3.5-turbo numbers.
Contamination is acknowledged only in Sec 4.4 as a general risk (pre-training corpora of foundation models are obscure); it is not checked for any benchmark or model in the tables.

Comparison fairness is not audited: many winners are task-specific fine-tunes (WizardMath, WizardCoder, MentaLlama, Radiology-Llama-2, Struc-Bench) compared against a general-purpose chat model; hallucination methods in Table 5 are inference-time pipelines wrapped around GPT-3.5-turbo or other models, each on a different benchmark.
Authors concede (Sec 4.4) that winners are mostly distilled from closed models plus expert annotation, which may mask whether the approach scales to the teacher.

LLM-judged benchmarks (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval) are used as headline evidence without discussion of judge bias. Some open models rank very differently across benchmarks (Zephyr-7B: strong MT-Bench, 52.15 on Open LLM Leaderboard).
Internal inconsistencies between text and tables (WizardCoder 19.1 vs 9.2 points; WizardMath 42.9 vs 24.5; Platypus ~20% vs 15.3 points; ZeroSCROLLS 37.7/36.7 not in Table 4).
Several cited winners are not open (InstructRetro is 'not yet open-sourced', footnote 7) and some leading models release no training details.
Dated: covers up to Nov 2023 (v4 Jan 2024); GPT-4 remains ahead on nearly all tables.
practices: Prefer a few high-quality, diverse SFT examples over volume: tens of thousands suffice, e.g. 27,540 annotations for Llama-2 (Sec 4.3).
Use PPO or DPO after SFT for alignment; distilled DPO lets Zephyr-7B approach 70B models on general benchmarks (Sec 4.3).
Exclude personal information from pre-training data (Sec 4.3).
Check pre-training corpus overlap with benchmarks and standardise disclosure of pre-training data to address contamination (Sec 4.4).
Use speculative decoding and vLLM for serving (Sec 4.3).
